name: Particle Accelerators
what: This subtopic covers how particle accelerators use electric fields to accelerate charged particles and magnetic fields to change their direction. It includes the electron gun, velocity selectors, mass spectrometers, and synchrotrons such as the Australian Synchrotron in Melbourne.
why: Particle accelerators are used in medical treatment (linear accelerators for cancer therapy), scientific research (synchrotrons), and diagnostics (mass spectrometers). This section brings together energy, electric field, and magnetic field concepts into a single applied context.

items.title: I can describe how an electron gun accelerates electrons and calculate the speed of electrons using qV = ½mv²
items.what: An electron gun heats a cathode to release electrons, which are then accelerated through a voltage V toward an anode. The work done by the electric field converts to kinetic energy: qV = ½mv², giving v = √(2qV/m).
items.why: The electron gun is the starting point for electron microscopes, cathode ray tubes, and linear accelerators. Understanding it connects electric potential energy to kinetic energy, unifying earlier parts of the course.
items.example: An electron accelerated from rest through 1000 V gains kinetic energy Ek = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 1000 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ J, and reaches a speed of v = √(2 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁶ / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 1.87 × 10⁷ m/s.

items.title: I can explain that electric fields change the speed of charged particles while magnetic fields change their direction
items.what: An electric field exerts a force along the direction of motion, doing work on the particle and changing its kinetic energy (speed). A magnetic field exerts a force perpendicular to the motion, which changes direction but does no work, so speed stays constant.
items.why: This is the key functional distinction between electric and magnetic fields in accelerators. Linear acceleration is done by electric fields; steering and containing the beam is done by magnetic fields.
items.example: In the Australian Synchrotron, electrons are first accelerated to high speed by electric fields in a linear accelerator, then directed in a circular path by strong magnetic fields. The magnetic fields cannot change the electrons' speed, only their direction.

items.title: I can explain how crossed electric and magnetic fields act as a velocity selector and derive the selected velocity v = E/B
items.what: When a charged particle passes through perpendicular electric and magnetic fields, the electric force (qE) and magnetic force (qvB) act in opposite directions. Only particles where these forces are equal (qE = qvB) travel straight, giving a selected velocity of v = E/B.
items.why: Velocity selectors allow only particles of a specific speed to pass into a detector or analyser. They are used in mass spectrometers and electron microscopes where a precise, known speed is required for accurate results.
items.example: In J.J. Thomson's experiment, he adjusted B until the beam was undeflected. With E = 2.0 × 10⁵ V/m and B = 0.10 T, the selected velocity was v = E/B = 2.0 × 10⁵ / 0.10 = 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s.

items.title: I can explain how a mass spectrometer uses electric and magnetic fields to separate ions by mass
items.what: In a mass spectrometer, ions are accelerated by an electric field to a known speed, then enter a magnetic field. The radius of their circular path depends on mass: r = mv/(qB). Lighter ions curve more tightly, heavier ions less so, separating them for detection.
items.why: Mass spectrometers are used to identify unknown compounds, measure molecular weights, detect trace substances, and even identify new virus strains. This is one of the most direct applications of the charged particle in a magnetic field formula.
items.example: Two isotopes of carbon (carbon-12 and carbon-14) entering the same magnetic field at the same speed will follow arcs of slightly different radii because their masses differ. The separation of where they land on a detector reveals which isotope is which.

items.title: I can describe the role of electric and magnetic fields in a synchrotron and explain why the magnetic field must increase as particles are accelerated
items.what: A synchrotron accelerates particles in a closed circular loop. Electric fields in straight sections increase the particle speed. Magnetic fields in curved sections keep the particles on the circular path. As speed increases, the magnetic field must increase to maintain a constant orbital radius (from r = mv/(qB), if v increases, B must also increase to keep r constant).
items.why: The Australian Synchrotron in Melbourne is a key example of this technology. Understanding synchrotrons shows how the formulas for circular motion, magnetic force, and energy all connect at the frontier of applied physics.
items.example: The Australian Synchrotron accelerates electrons to 99.99999% of the speed of light, increasing the magnetic field progressively to keep them in the 70 m diameter ring. The resulting radiation (from infrared to X-ray) is used for medical and materials research.
